p.x:
In my family, we try to save water and power. My mum says, "Don't leave the tap on when you brush your teeth!" We take a short shower instead of a bath, because a bath uses much more water.
My brother and I wash the dishes in a bowl, not under running water. We also drink water from the tap; my dad put a filter on it, so it's clean and safe.
When we leave a room, we always turn off the light switch. My little sister made a sign for the door: "Turn off the lights!" Last month, our electricity bill was much lower. My mum was very happy!

p.t: Where Does Our Energy Come From?
p.x:
Every time you switch on a light, the power comes from a power station. In Thailand, much of our electricity is generated by burning gas. In the past, many countries also used a lot of coal and oil. These are called fossil fuels, and they produce pollution and carbon dioxide.
Today, cleaner energy is becoming more popular. Solar panels on roofs use the sun to make electricity, and a wind farm uses the wind. Some countries also use nuclear power, although many people worry about its safety.
Water is important for energy, too. A dam across a river creates a large reservoir, and the moving water produces electricity. But in a dry year, there may be a water shortage, and some villages still depend on a well.
At home, we can all help to conserve energy. Air conditioning and heating use the most electricity, so set them carefully. Check your meter to see your consumption, and choose efficient machines. During a blackout, you'll realise how much we depend on electricity! If a pipe leaks, call a plumber quickly, and remember that bottled water creates plastic waste.

Water and energy are closely linked, a relationship experts call the 'water-energy nexus'. Producing energy requires vast amounts of water: power stations need it for cooling, and hydroelectric dams depend on rivers that are increasingly affected by drought. At the same time, supplying clean water requires energy, to pump groundwater, treat sewage and, in some regions, run desalination plants that turn seawater into drinking water.
This link creates difficult choices. In parts of the Middle East, where fresh water is scarce, desalination provides most of the drinking supply, but it consumes enormous amounts of electricity, often generated from fossil fuels. Elsewhere, farmers pump so much groundwater for crops that underground supplies are falling faster than rain can replace them. In severe droughts, some cities have been forced to ration water, limiting how much each household can use.
Renewable energy offers part of the solution. Wind turbines and solar farms need very little water once built, and connecting them to a smart national grid can balance supply and demand. Pricing also matters: tariffs that charge more at peak times encourage people to use electricity when it is plentiful, while a smart thermostat can reduce waste automatically.
Individuals, too, can reduce their carbon footprint and their water use at the same time, for example by shortening showers, which saves both water and the energy needed to heat it. In the end, experts argue, we cannot solve one problem without considering the other.
